newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Ceremony remembers French casualties in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Ceremony remembers French casualties in Bosnia.

text.p: Sixty eight French peacekeepers who died while serving in the United Nations mission in former Yugoslavia were honored in an emotional ceremony on Wednesday by their families and fellow officers.

Six families who lost their kin in Bosnia flew from France to Sarajevo to attend a mass at the main cathedral and to dedicate a plaque to the dead soldiers. Most were killed during a 3-1/2 year war in Bosnia.
The parents of the last to be killed, Captain Gilles Carreau, who died in July 1995 after serving three weeks in Bosnia, said Sarajevo held a special meaning for them.
"This is the city in which my son lived his last moments. I think he was happy here and I came to Sarajevo to find my son again," Carreau's mother Josiane said.
His father Jean-Claude, a retired bank clerk, had founded a nation-wide association of parents and friends of victims who took part in intervention in former Yugoslavia (ANPAVI).
"Today, Sarajevo is more than a name for me. It is a passion. I will continue what my son did," he said.
A plaque with sixty-eight engraved names was erected on Tuesday at the entrance to the Sarajevo airport where three French officers were killed in April 1995 by an artillery shell.
French peacekeepers controlled the airport throughout the 1992-1997 war which enabled the delivery of the humanitarian aid to beseiged Sarajevo.
"Nobody should forget this happened," Jean-Claude Carreau said after the plaque was unveiled.
NATO peacekeepers replaced U.N. soldiers in Bosnia after the fighting ended with a peace accord in December 1995. France contributes about 3,000 soldiers to NATO's Stabilisation Forces (SFOR).
Several French soldiers serving as NATO peacekeepers have died during the past 16 months in various accidents but not from hostile fire.
